content: The systematic collection, analysis, and interpretation of entomological data are essential for assessing risks, planning, implementing, monitoring, and evaluating vector control interventions. This process is critical for public health surveillance and the effective management of vector-borne diseases. Targeted drug administration involves providing a complete treatment course of antimalarial medication to individuals who are at a higher risk of malaria infection compared to the general population. This approach aims to reduce the disease burden in vulnerable groups. Targeted testing and treatment refer to the parasitological screening of individuals at increased risk of malaria infection. Those who test positive for malaria are treated accordingly, ensuring that resources are directed toward those in need. Malaria diagnostic testing is used to confirm whether an individual has a malaria infection. This ensures accurate diagnosis and appropriate treatment. Tolerance describes a reduced response in a human or mosquito host to a specific level of infection, toxin, or drug, which is less than what is typically expected. Transmission intensity is defined as the frequency at which individuals in a specific area are bitten by Anopheles mosquitoes carrying human malaria sporozoites. The transmission season refers to the time of year when the majority of mosquito-borne malaria infections occur. This period is influenced by environmental and climatic factors. Re-establishment of transmission occurs when there is a measurable incidence of locally acquired malaria infections in an area where transmission had previously been interrupted. This is due to repeated cycles of mosquito-borne infections. Interruption of transmission is achieved when mosquito-borne malaria transmission ceases in a specific geographical area as a result of effective antimalarial measures. Perennial transmission refers to malaria transmission that occurs consistently throughout the year, with minimal variation in intensity. Residual transmission describes the persistence of malaria transmission despite the implementation of a highly effective malaria control program. This can occur due to factors such as insecticide resistance or behavioral changes in mosquito populations. Seasonal transmission is characterized by malaria transmission that occurs only during certain months of the year, with significantly reduced transmission during other months. Stable transmission is an epidemiological pattern of malaria characterized by a consistent prevalence rate with little variation from year to year, except in cases of rapid scaling up of interventions or significant environmental changes. Unstable transmission is an epidemiological pattern of malaria characterized by large variations in incidence rates from one year to another. A mosquito trap is a device designed to capture mosquitoes, either with or without attractant components such as light, carbon dioxide, living baits, or suction mechanisms. Treatment failure refers to the inability to clear malarial parasitemia or prevent recrudescence after administering an antimalarial medication, regardless of whether clinical symptoms are resolved. Anti-relapse treatment is a specific type of antimalarial therapy aimed at eliminating hypnozoites to prevent relapses or late primary infections caused by Plasmodium vivax or Plasmodium ovale. Directly observed treatment (DOT) involves administering treatment under the direct supervision of a healthcare worker to ensure adherence and effectiveness. First-line treatment is the recommended therapy in national treatment guidelines, considered the preferred choice for managing malaria. Second-line treatment is used when first-line therapy fails or in patients who are allergic to or unable to tolerate the first-line treatment. Presumptive treatment involves administering antimalarial drugs to individuals with suspected malaria without prior diagnostic testing or before blood examination results are available. Preventive treatment refers to the intermittent administration of a full therapeutic course of antimalarial medication, either alone or in combination, to prevent malarial illness by maintaining therapeutic drug levels in the blood during periods of high risk. Radical treatment aims to achieve a complete cure of malaria. This approach is specific to infections caused by Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium ovale and involves using medications that target both blood and liver stages of the parasite. The trophozoite stage of malaria parasites represents their development within host red blood cells, transitioning from the ring stage to just before nuclear division. Trophozoites contain visible malaria pigment, which can be observed microscopically. Principal vectors are the primary Anopheles species responsible for malaria transmission in a given setting. Secondary or subsidiary vectors are Anopheles species that play a lesser role in malaria transmission but are still capable of maintaining transmission at a reduced level. Vectorial capacity refers to the number of new infections that a given vector population can induce per case per day in a specific location and time, assuming the human population remains fully susceptible to malaria. Vigilance is a public health function aimed at preventing the reintroduction of malaria. It involves close monitoring for any occurrence of malaria in receptive areas and implementing necessary measures to prevent the re-establishment of transmission.
